summary:
I've been chasing down a power fault on my AI box — a Ryzen desktop running a Tesla P100 that serves local LLM inference for a handful of my other projects. It died cold, no warning, no kernel panic, no thermal trip, nothing in the logs to point at. Swapping the PSU fixed it, but before I trusted that I wrote a load-test harness that pushed the card to its full 250W rated draw for 49 minutes with repeated load-drop/reload cycles, then checked ECC error counts, retired pages, and prefill latency drift for any sign of degradation. Clean on every axis. The annoying part wasn't the fix, it was proving a fix with no smoking gun — you're stuck substituting parts and hoping the problem doesn't come back.

That machine also runs a small FastAPI proxy I built to deal with the fact that only one model can live on the GPU's 16GB at a time. It watches everything that wants the card — a couple of different LLM backends, an image generation pipeline — and serializes access: evict whoever's resident, wait for VRAM to actually drop, then hand the card to whoever's waiting. The interesting bug there was a warm-model fast path: one backend holds its memory persistently even when idle, so the generic "wait for VRAM to settle" logic would time out on every single request against it, adding ten seconds to something that should've taken half a second. Once I special-cased "if this backend's already loaded, skip the eviction dance," a routine turn dropped from 16 seconds to about 5.

I also finally looked at four months of power-draw data I'd been logging and never actually read. Wrote a small dashboard for it — plain SVG charts, no charting library, has to run fully offline on my LAN. The one design choice worth mentioning: gaps in the data are drawn as gaps, not smoothed over, because the whole reason I built the thing was to catch a logger that had silently stopped running for two weeks and nobody noticed. Numbers came back roughly in line with what I'd estimated going in, which was oddly satisfying.

Smaller thing: a barbell rep counter built on a cheap ESP32 camera module, tracking colored plates to count reps on-device, no cloud round-trip, with a tiny local dashboard to see the count live.

highlights.oneLiner: Fixed a warm-model fast path so cached backend calls skip the eviction wait, cutting latency 16s to 5s.
ESP32-camera barbell rep counter tracking colored plates on-device, with a local live-count dashboard.
